title: Medieval philosophy
audience: a college student in a philosophy degree program, or an adult studying the same material on their own
purpose: Study philosophy from late antiquity to the fourteenth century in the Christian, Islamic and Jewish traditions: Augustine, Boethius, al-Farabi, Avicenna, Averroes, Maimonides, Anselm, Aquinas, Duns Scotus and Ockham on God, being and essence, universals, the soul, time, providence and free will, and faith and reason.
primary_reading: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Medieval Philosophy (free)

weeks.2: Augustine on time, evil and free will
weeks.4: The problem of universals: Porphyry and Boethius
weeks.5: Philosophy in the Islamic world: al-Farabi and Avicenna on essence and existence
weeks.6: Averroes and Maimonides: faith, reason and the eternity of the world
weeks.9: Aquinas on being, essence and the soul

blocks.deliverable: Reconstruct the foreknowledge problem and Boethius's reply.
Explain Avicenna's distinction between essence and existence.
Week 7 midterm; reconstruct the ontological argument and Gaunilo's reply.
Compare Aquinas and Scotus on what makes something an individual.
Defend realism or nominalism about universals in two pages.
Submit the project; take an unseen 120 minute final in week 14.

project: Medieval disputation: write a disputed question in the medieval style on one topic (universals, essence and existence, or foreknowledge): state the question, give three objections, a sed contra, your answer with arguments drawn from at least two medieval thinkers, and a reply to each objection, about 2,000 words in all.
completion: finish the project, take the week 7 midterm and week 14 cumulative final, then complete a new cumulative assessment after 1 to 2 weeks. Explain one major idea aloud without notes.
